newsitem.title: USA: Prospective buyers tour Disney newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Prospective buyers tour Disney newspaper.

text.p: Four media companies toured the offices of the Kansas City Star newspaper this week with an interest in buying it and other properties owned by Walt Disney Co, sources said on Wednesday.
A story published Wednesday in the Star said representatives of Tribune Co, Times Mirror Co, Knight-Ridder Inc and Hearst Corp visited the Star's offices this week.
"The story in this morning's paper had no inaccuracies," a spokesman for the Star said, declining to comment further on the report.
Disney said in January that it would explore options related to the publishing operations of Capital Cities/ABC, including a possible sale of the business.

Industry analysts said Disney's publishing assets, which include a variety of newspapers and industry publications such as Women's Wear Daily, Automotive Marketing and Institutional Investor, could fetch as much as $2.5 billion.

Disney's publishing assets also include the Fort Worth Star-Telegram newspaper. John Morton, a media consultant in Maryland, speculated that Hearst might be attracted to that paper since it already owns papers in Houston and San Antonio.
Morton said he was surprised to see Times Mirror and Tribune Co on the list of possible suitors.

"Times Mirror's been downsizing and vigorously combatting costs and trying to improve its return on equity... and of course taking on a major acquisition like that would slow that process down," Morton said.
"Tribune Company is absorbing its huge acquistion of Renaissance Broadcasting. It was a little surprise that they would be stepping forward," Morton said.
Morton said he also expected Cox Enterprises, parent company of Cox Communications Inc, may show interest in Disney's publications.
Analysts questioned whether Disney might try to sell off the entire group to one single buyer or whether the company would try to split up the sale.

James C. Goss, media and entertainment analyst with Nesbitt Burns Securities in Chicago, said he saw scope for Disney to sell its newspapers separately because major-market newspapers were in high demand but rarely went up for sale in such a public fashion.
"It's more likely to me that (the sale) would be in separate components, and at most they might be grouped by category, but possibly even individual properties," Goss said.
"I would think that selling Kansas City separately from Fort Worth would probably make sense," Goss said. "If it were magazines, there might be some logical way to group magazines by a buyer."
